## Notebook-first workflow

All model-edit steps are maintained as Python scripts and should be run in order:

```sh
make 01   # Non-muscle edits
make 02   # Muscle edits
make 03   # Bilateral mirroring
```

These scripts generate the final files:

- `models/output/`
  - `rat_hindlimb_unilateral.osim`
  - `rat_hindlimb_unilateral_no_muscles.osim`
  - `rat_hindlimb_bilateral.osim`
  - `rat_hindlimb_bilateral_no_muscles.osim`

This Quarto document is narrative-only and does not execute code during render.

## Modernize Johnson Model

Original model drawn from a [SimTK project](https://simtk.org/projects/rat_hlimb_model) which is based on Johnson et al. 2008 [@johnsonMusculoskeletalModelRat].

Non-muscle edits (naming conventions, geometry format updates, coordinate locks, knee frame/transform updates, and marker-set updates) are executed in [pipeline/01_non_muscle_edits.py](pipeline/01_non_muscle_edits.py).

## Knee joint definition

In Johnson's original model, the tibia offset frame used as the parent frame for the knee joint is defined at the distal end of the tibia, and the spatial transform is handled by a `SimmSpline` component. When the model is scaled to subject-specific parameters, the knee motion is incorrect because the `SimmSpline` trajectory does not change, and the tibia offset frame does not move, so there is nothing to account for the new tibia length.

To fix this, we adjust the tibia offset frame to be at the approximate joint center of the knee as determined by the instantaneous center of rotation (ICR) of the knee shown in @fig-knee.

![Knee ICR](./figs/knee-icr.png){#fig-knee}

## Muscle path analysis

The model is moved through its full range of motion and muscle lengths are analyzed to identify discontinuities that may indicate problems with muscle path definitions. The `OsimGraph` class from [`osimpy`](https://github.com/hudsonburke/osimpy), a collection of tools for OpenSim analysis using Python, is used to represent an OpenSim model as a graph structure, which allows for efficient analysis of muscle paths.

### Discontinuous muscles

The following muscles were identified as having discontinuous length changes:

- BFa
- CF
- STp
- TA
- VL

Investigating the root cause of this, we found that the likely culprit is a hard-coded value in [OpenSim's WrapCylinder.cpp code](https://github.com/opensim-org/opensim-core/blob/f9cd558ec3ea99dda206e5e412e62e23cf19bd7e/OpenSim/Simulation/Wrap/WrapCylinder.cpp#L668) that determines the number of segments used to approximate the muscle path over a wrapping cylinder:

```c
// Each muscle segment on the surface of the cylinder should be
// 0.002 meters long. This assumes the model is in meters, of course.
int numWrapSegments = (int)(aWrapResult.wrap_path_length / 0.002);
if (numWrapSegments < 1) numWrapSegments = 1;
```

This means that for cylinders with small circumferences, the muscle path may be approximated with very few segments, leading to abrupt changes in path length as the muscle wraps around the cylinder. To address this issue, we either need to modify the OpenSim source code to increase the number of segments used for wrapping or modify the wrapping paths in the model.

### Muscle path redefinition

Johnson's original model relied heavily on wrapping surfaces, but a more recent work that built upon that original model and drew from Greene's [@greeneAnatomyRat] original anatomical text defined a large set of attachment points for muscles instead of relying on wrapping surfaces [@youngNeuromechanicalRatModel2018]. This newer model may avoid some of the issues with discontinuous muscle lengths. Unfortunately, that model was created for a software called [Animatlab](https://www.animatlab.com/), and there was no existing OpenSim version of it.

We were able to get in touch with the author of the Animatlab model, Dr. Young, who provided the original files and assisted in understanding the model structure.

Muscle-specific edits (Thelen-to-Millard conversion, wrap/path redefinition, parameter updates, and unilateral outputs) are executed in [pipeline/02_muscle_edits.py](pipeline/02_muscle_edits.py).


## Estimate tendon slack length

Tendon slack length (TSL) is one of the most influential parameters in muscle force production, yet anatomical measurements are notoriously inaccurate. We estimate TSL using the method of Manal & Buchanan (2004), extended to multiple muscles by Ramalingasetty et al. (2021).

### Method

The approach uses observed muscle-tendon lengths during motion to find a single TSL that is consistent across all sampled poses. For each muscle at each walking pose, the muscle-tendon length (LMT) is computed from the model kinematics. The optimizer then jointly finds:

1. **Fiber length at each pose** — constrained to the normalized range [0.6, 1.5] × lm_opt
2. **A single shared TSL** — enforced across all poses simultaneously

The objective minimizes the mismatch between the geometric tendon length (LMT − fiber × cos(pennation)) and the tendon length implied by the muscle's force-equilibrium curves, subject to a no-buckling constraint (tendon length ≥ slack length at every pose).

Walking kinematics are sampled at resolution=5 (5 points per coordinate per timestep, mean ± 2 standard deviations across 202 timesteps), then averaged back to one LMT per timestep before optimization. This captures the walking variability while keeping the optimizer tractable (201 variables per muscle).

Implementation: [pipeline/04_tsl_optimization.py](pipeline/04_tsl_optimization.py) calls `optimize_fiber_length_and_tsl` from the [`tsl-optimization`](https://github.com/hudsonburke/tsl-optimization) package.

### Comparison with measured values

The table below compares our optimized TSL against anatomical measurements from Johnson et al. (2011) and Eng et al. (2008). Johnson reports TSL from direct tendon measurement; Eng reports fiber length (Lf) and total muscle length (Lm), from which we can compute the expected TSL fraction.

| Muscle | Johnson lts (mm) | Eng Lf/Lm | Optimized TSL (mm) |
|--------|-----------------:|----------:|-------------------:|
| EDL    | 9.0              | 0.48      | 38.9               |
| FDL    | 8.7              | 0.30      | 45.1               |
| FHL    | 9.7              | 0.51      | 40.7               |
| Sol    | 9.5              | 0.69      | 21.2               |
| TA     | 11.9             | 0.57      | 21.4               |
| LG     | 9.4              | 0.46      | 30.2               |
| MG     | 9.1              | 0.45      | 29.6               |
| TP     | 12.4             | 0.23      | 36.1               |
| Pla    | 6.7              | 0.34      | 30.0               |
| Per    | 12.7             | 0.32      | 37.0               |
| VL     | 6.6              | 0.57      | 20.0               |
| VM     | 6.6              | 0.61      | 24.0               |
| RF     | —                | —         | 24.8               |
| STa    | —                | —         | 9.0                |
| BFa    | —                | —         | 5.0                |

Results are written to `data/parameters/tsl_comparison.csv` by `make 04`.

### Why our values differ from Johnson's

Our optimized TSL values are consistently larger than Johnson's measured values. This is expected and results from two factors:

1. **Different muscle paths.** Johnson's model uses wrapping surfaces; ours uses Young's via-point attachment points. The via-point paths are longer for many muscles (e.g., EDL's path is 55mm vs ~37mm in Johnson's model) because they route through intermediate bodies rather than wrapping over surfaces.

2. **Different lm_opt / LMT ratios.** Johnson's optimal fiber lengths were designed for Johnson's shorter paths. With longer paths, the fiber (capped at 1.5 × lm_opt) cannot account for the extra length, so TSL absorbs the difference.

The optimized TSL values are correct *given the model's muscle paths*. To reduce them, the muscle paths themselves would need to be shortened (e.g., by adjusting via-point positions or the mesh registration that maps Young's coordinates to Johnson's frame).

Any tendon slack lengths estimated as ≤ 0 are set to rigid tendon compliance.
